adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The archive room of the county courthouse had not been opened in nearly a decade. Dust lay over the shelves in a pale film, and the clerk, a patient woman named Agnes, had spent three weeks cataloguing boxes that nobody had requested. Most of the files concerned property disputes from the 1930s, their pages brittle and their handwriting faded to a thin brown script. She worked slowly, reading each folder before she shelved it, because the alternative was silence.

On the morning of the fourteenth she found a bundle tied with string and labelled in red pencil. Inside were transcripts from a civil suit brought by a shipping family against the harbour board. The testimony was lengthy, and the arguments turned, as far as she could tell, on whether a storm could be called an act of God when the forecast had been printed in the newspaper the day before.

The harbour board had kept its own records in a set of ledgers bound in green cloth. Agnes found them in the same box, stacked beneath the transcripts, and spent an hour comparing the entries with the dates in the testimony. The figures agreed, which surprised her, and the signatures did not, which did not.

The judge who heard the case was impressed by neither side. In his written decision he complained about the quality of the evidence, the vagueness of the witnesses, and the habit both counsel had of repeating themselves. He concluded that the loss of the cargo was the fault of no one in particular, that the insurers had already paid what they owed, and that each party should bear its own costs. Then, near the end, he added the sentence Agnes would remember: the judge wrote that "the evidence is thin" (R v. Hale 1994) and that the court declined to speculate further.

Agnes copied the sentence into her notebook. She had no legal training, but she understood the tone. It was the tone of a man asked to decide something impossible who had decided to say as little as possible. She closed the folder, tied the string, and carried it back to the shelf. Outside, the rain had stopped and the street reflected the last of the light. She locked the door, signed the register, and walked home along the river, thinking about how many of the files she had read that year had ended in the same way, with a sentence that gave nothing away and a signature that closed the matter.

By the time she reached her street the lamps were lit. In the kitchen she made tea, opened the notebook, and read the sentence again. "The evidence is thin." She wondered, briefly, who Hale had been and why his name should stand beside the words of a judge in a county she had never left. Then she turned off the light and went upstairs, and the archive room settled back into its dust.
